Expression of programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) is frequently observed in human cancers. Binding of
PD-L1 to its receptor PD-1 on activated T cells inhibits anti-tumor immunity by counteracting T cell-activating
signals. Antibody-based PD-1-PD-L1 inhibitors can induce durable tumor remissions in patients with diverse
advanced cancers, and thus expression of PD-L1 on tumor cells and other cells in the tumor microenwiroment
is of major clinical relevance. Here we review the roles of the PD-1-PD-L1 axis in cancer, focusing on recent
findings on the mechanisms that regulate PD-L1 expression at the transcriptional, posttranscriptional, and
protein level. We place this knowledge in the context of observations in the clinic and discuss how it may

inform the design of more precise and effective cancer immune checkpoint therapies.

Introduction
‘The T cell-based immune system has evolved to recognize and,
destroy aberrant cells, such as pathogen-infected cells and,
ccancer cells. Detection of such aberrant calls occurs through
binging ofthe T cell receptor (TCR) on T cells to peptide-major
bistocompatibility complexes (MHO) on target calls. However,
the outcome of this interaction is toa very large extent controlled
by a series of co-stimulatory and co-inhibitory receptors and,
their ligands (also known as immune checkpoints). By regulating
the quantity and functional activity of antigen-specific T cell
these checkpoint pathways play a critical role in limiting tissue
{damage and maintenance of set-tolerance.
‘Among alimmune checkpoints, the PD-L1-PD-1 pathway has
‘stood out because ofits proven vaiue as a therapeutic target in a
large number of malignancies. At present, antibodies targeting
the PD-L1-PD-1 axisare being evaluated in more than 1,000 clin-
ical trials and have been approved for cancers including mela
‘noma, non-small cell ung cancer (NSCLC), renal cell carcinoma
(RCC), Hodgkin's lymphoma, bladder cancer, head and neck
‘Squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCO), Merkel-cell carcinoma,
‘and microsatellite instable-high (MSI-H) or mismatch repair-defi-
cient (GMMR) solid tumors. Despite the considerable improve-
‘ment in patient outcome that has been achieved with PD-L1~
PD-1 blockade, durable responses to these therapies are
‘observed in only a minority of patients and intrinsic therapy resis
tance is common. In some tumor types, expression of PD-L1 on,
‘tumor cells and in the tumor microenvironment has been associ
‘ated with clinical response, highlighting the need for a better un-
derstanding of the processes that regulate PD-L1 expression.
In this review, we first discuss the fundamental biology of the
PD-L1-PD-1 immune checkpoint. We then describe the promise
‘and limitations of current ant-PO-L1-PD-1 therapies and the
relevance of PD-L1 expression in predicting clinical response.
‘Subsequently, we cover the current understanding of the molec
ular mechanisms that control such PD-L1 expression. In this,
‘section we dissect the complex regulatory network that detor-
‘mines PD-L1 levels into five major components that involve (1)
‘genomic aberrations, 2) inflammatory signaling, (3) oncogenic
signaling, (4) microRNA-based control, and (5) posttransational,

The PD-L1-PD-1 Axis: Structure and Function
Programmed cell death protein 1 (PO-1; also called CD279) is
tone of the co-inhibitory receptors that is expressed on the sur-
face of antigen-stimulated T cells (shia et a. 1992).PD-1 inter-
acts with two ligands, PO-L1 (CD274) and PD-L2 (C0273).
Expression of PO-L2 is observed on, for instance, macrophages,
Cs, and mast cells. PD-L1 expression can be detected on he-
‘matopoietc cells including T cells, B cells, macrophages. den-
tic cols (OCs), and mast cells, and non-hematopoietic healthy
tissue colls including vascular endothelial coll, keratinocytes,
pancreatic islet cels, astrocytes, placenta syncytiotrophoblast
Cells, and comeal epithelial and endothelial ces. Both PD-Lt
‘and PO-L2 can be expressed by tumor cells and tumor stroma.
Engagement of PD-L2 at such tumor sites may potentially
Contribute to PD-t-mediated T cell inhibition (Yesrley et al
2017). However, to date, there is no compelling evidence indi-
cating that antibodies against PD-1, which block binding to
both PD-L1 and PD-L2, show higher clinical activity than ant-
bodies against PD-L1. These data are consistent with a model
in which PD-Lt is the dominant inhibitory ligand of PD-1 on
cell in the human tumor microenvironment.
Both PD-1 and PD-L1 are typeI transmembrane proteins that
belong to the immunoglobulin lg) superfamily. PO-1 consists of
fan ig-V lke extracellular domain, a transmembrane domain, and
‘cytoplasmic domain that harbors two tyrosine-based signaling
‘motifs (shia et al, 1982: Zhang etal, 2004) PD-L1 contains an
Ig-V and Ig-C-Ike extracelular domain, a transmembrane
domain, and a short cytoplasmic tail that does not contain ca-
‘onical signaling motifs (Dong et a. 1999; Keir etal. 2008; Lin
tal, 2008). Interactions between the extracellular domains of
PD-L1 and PO-1 can induce a conformational change in PD-1
that leads to phosphorylation of the cytoplasmic immunorecep-
tor tyrosine-based inhibitory motif (TIM) and the immunorecep-
tor tyrosine-based switch motif (TSM) by Src family kinases
(Gauen ot al, 1994; Straus and Weiss, 1982; Zak et al, 2015).
